children: America's patchwork of retirement savings vehicles aren't cutting it anymore. Lawmakers have a unique opportunity to correct the system.
One clear message from the midterms: Voters are tired of hearing how well the economy is doing when they are living with a deep-seated sense of financial insecurity.

Most Americans don't feel that the growth in our economy is personally benefitting them. To a large degree, they're right. Over the past few decades, our country's extraordinary economic growth has disproportionately benefited the wealthy.

Some of this reflects structural changes. For generations, homeownership and pensions helped middle-class Americans build wealth that grew in tandem with the broader economy. Today, few workers have traditional pensions, and homeownership is increasingly out of reach as housing stock and affordability fall to multidecade lows and mortgage rates creep higher.
Correcting for these disappearing sources of wealth will require policy changes. One very obvious place to start is retirement, a truly bipartisan issue that drives affordability sentiment.

Right now, our country's retirement system consists of a patchwork of investment programs: 401(k)s tied to specific jobs, individual brokerage accounts, digital trading (which can often be highly speculative), state-sponsored retirement programs, and the new Trump Accounts — none of which is likely to cover one's retirement costs on their own.

Those who do best under the existing system have access to strong company plans with generous matching, as well as substantial personal investments. But that isn't the reality for many workers in our service-oriented gig economy. Among those with a W-2 job, saving or investing enough to retire comfortably by age 65 feels more difficult than ever. And Social Security, a program not designed to fully fund retirement, typically replaces only about 40% of preretirement earnings.

It's time to create a coordinated, permanent national retirement system, and the next Congress has a unique opportunity to make it happen. They will be working with both a strong mandate to make affordability reforms and a president who has demonstrated interest in broadening access to financial markets.

They should start by enhancing the bipartisan 2025 Retirement Savings for America Act, which proposed to expand retirement savings to workers without employer-sponsored plans, into a broader National Retirement Act. The program would connect with workplace plans and individual accounts so Americans can invest seamlessly throughout their lives. It would use the infrastructure developed by the government for Trump Accounts to create a retirement savings program for workers who don't have access to a 401(k), with automatic enrollment, matching contributions from the government, and low-cost investment options.

Within the financial services industry, there is some skepticism about heavy government involvement in retirement savings. But a national system would ideally be a public-private partnership. Government would set common standards and tax incentives for individuals and employers, and investment firms would manage the accounts and offer low-cost, diversified investments.

Private workplace plans would remain the backbone of the program, but employers would now be steered to national standards for automatic employee enrollment and employer contributions. Congress could tie corporate tax incentives to retirement benefits by requiring companies that receive those tax benefits to provide meaningful employer contributions. Workers without workplace plans would automatically enroll in the national plan.

Importantly, the account would follow the individual. Today's workforce is much more mobile than in the past. People change jobs more frequently, take on side gigs, and move between traditional employment and self-employment. Someone who starts working in California and moves to Texas shouldn't have to figure out a different way to save for retirement. Their account should simply follow them. A national system could make that the standard for everyone.
